extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of democratic politics and civic culture (aspiring leaders, critics, intellectuals, educators)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance about how individual excellence, leadership, criticism, and education should be cultivated and exercised to promote democratic social reconstruction and the fulfillment of the American national Promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: High technical competence (individual excellence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual excellence is defined exclusively in terms of high but special technical competence; the formative individual must seek increase of his individuality by competent and disinterested special work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes specialized skill and excellence as the foundation for social influence: 'competent individual instruments' are prerequisites for political and social reorganization. This competence should be genuine, distinctive, and manifest in performances that can attract appreciation even from a small audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-discipline and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals capable of edifying practical leadership must be disciplined and trained; they must be a product of self-discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social and political reorganization is 'a delusion' unless individuals with disciplined training exist. The individual must begin and carry as far as he can the work of his own emancipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness in special work
rubrics_metrics.description: The formative individual should be disinterested (not primarily motivated by personal gain) in the pursuit of special technical excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'competent and disinterested special work' recurs; disinterestedness supports moral authority and makes the individual's achievements more socially formative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative must come from individuals (not solely collective action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The initiative for individual and social improvement cannot be left to collective action; the individual must begin the work of his own emancipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that while individual and social improvement are mutually dependent, the individual must take the first step — collective majorities alone are insufficient to generate the needed leaders and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must be willing to love and serve fellow-countrymen (moral disposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fulfillment of the national Promise, individuals must love and wish to serve their fellow-countrymen and be prepared to reorganize economic, political, and social institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral sympathy is necessary in the long run, though the immediate formation of leaders may be grounded more in competence than explicit idealism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid naïve reliance on majority opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Securing a permanent popular majority in favor of a policy is not by itself sufficient; majorities composed of ordinary convinced adherents may render a project impossible in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (French republics) are used to argue that majorities without the right temper of practical competence and patriotism can produce counterproductive results.

rubrics_metrics.name: To exert social influence, specialists must become popular by making their work interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: The admirably competent individual cannot exercise constructive social influence unless he becomes popular; thus he must learn to express his better message in a popularly interesting manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument, reproaches, lectures, associations, or persuasion alone will not convert the public; the 'good thing' must be made to look good. This requires skill in presentation without necessarily compromising standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not compromise integrity for popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspiring leaders should not haul down the flag of their own individual purpose to obtain popular appreciation; if they do so they are unworthy to lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While making work attractive to the public is necessary, the individual must 'keep his flag flying at any personal cost or sacrifice.' Occasional incompatibility between purity of purpose and popularity is an acceptable risk of genuine enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a special public through distinctive excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: An exceptional practitioner who insists on doing his very best may create a small but influential following because his work possesses distinctive individual merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive quality attracts a few who then generate approving opinion and new clients who want that particular individual; this builds independent authority and helps popularize better standards more widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance, risk-taking, and willingness to sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Building a following and achieving genuine excellence involves real risks, sacrifices, and possibly wasted effort; resolute tenacity is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the architect who rejects many jobs and spends more on accepted jobs than profitable. Failures will occur even with deserving effort, but shirking and blaming the public indicates lack of necessary will and ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must guard against their followers and remain self-critical
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader must always be somewhat on his guard against his followers; the leadership that gains success is also a dangerous temptation and liable to become perverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because followers can tempt leaders away from original purposes, leaders must conscientiously reckon the actual cost of popular success and maintain vigilance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Followers must scrutinize leaders to prevent perverse leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Followers in a democracy must keep a sharp lookout lest their leaders be leading them astray.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual vigilance is part of democratic health: leaders must guard against followers, and followers must guard against leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational institutions should prepare competent individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Society's best assistance at present is to establish good schools of preliminary instruction to form competent individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools can provide the preliminary training needed; beyond that, exceptional individuals must impose themselves on the public to create followings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's competence, disinterestedness, and public role
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must be competent, disinterested, and his business is to make the public conscious of the extent of individual successes or failures and the reasons therefor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When standards improve, the critic gains larger public and more substantial material. He popularizes and explains admirable performance, embodies its significance, and acts as a 'lantern' illuminating the path rather than pretending to have all answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's aggressiveness against intellectual insincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should carry on an incessant and relentless warfare on prevailing intellectual insincerity — stabbing at popular indifference, sentimentality, and complacency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic may be 'more unscrupulous and aggressive' than other performers; he should 'stab away' to awaken public consciousness even if immediate constructive achievement is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral feeling (brotherhood) is necessary but insufficient without competence and reorganization
rubrics_metrics.description: A profound sense of human brotherhood is no substitute for specific efficiency; consummate faith alone cannot replace the slow process of social reorganization and individual discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evangelism without groundwork produces only temporary conversions; large-scale democratic fulfillment requires both moral feeling and technical/social work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy requires balance: individual independence and responsible exercise of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy compels insistence that individual power shall not be perversely or irresponsibly exercised; simultaneously it should not equate responsible power with mediocrity and dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The vitality of democracy depends on keeping both demands vigorous: assert independence while redeeming responsibility. Reconciliation of individual and popular interest is achieved by victorious individual or national contrivance, not by automatic formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement proceeds by experimental contrivance and iterative learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Social and individual amelioration is a matter of intelligent experimental contrivance based on immediate conditions; experiments must continue indefinitely and be candidly learned from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress is partial, costly, and requires experiments that are based on lessons from past failures and achievements. Creed and practice must be constantly modified to meet new experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising public standards requires leaders to make better things look good
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way popular standards can be improved is for those with higher standards to make their better message attractive and 'look good' to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improving tastes is an active task: leaders must 'mold their followers after their own likeness' and create a public rather than expect one to exist ready-made. Mere argumentation or reproach will not suffice.
